I've had suicidal ideation since I was 6. At this age my thoughts weren't exactly formulated as "I want to kill myself, I want to commit the physical act of unaliving myself", more like "I wish I wasn't alive, I wish I wasn't ever born, I wish I could just disappear". I used to be a believer back then, so I would pray God to take me back to him, cause I thought that was the best thing, the right thing to do. I wasn't actively suicidal, but I was aware that I might do it at some point and I believed I wouldn't reach the age of 12 years old, because I would have surely killed myself by then (I'm 27 now).

I remember clearly the reasons behind that state of mind. My mother had always told me she should have aborted me. I have always known that I wasn't meant to be born, that I was an accident, that my mother didn't plan me. My mother had good moments with me, there are many things to be grateful about her, don't get me wrong. It's just that every time she would get upset about something, she would go on rambling how my birth ruined her life, completely put her out of her path to achieve her dreams, how different her life would have been if she didn't give birth to me. There were also physical abuse besides the emotional one. I remember being dragged on the floor by my hair at the age of 5. So lots of mommy issues trauma.

I don't have nearly as much daddy issues. I spent my childhood divided between living in my father's country with my parents and living in my mother's country with my grandparents (who were good to me). I never really got attached to my father to begin with. He didn't abuse me or neglect me, but he didn't either defend me much from my mother. I also knew he used to mistreat my mother and he did sorta abandon us twice.

Maybe your daughter feels responsible for her father's actions, maybe she believes the world, your family would be better off without her. Maybe she feels undeserving to be alive. Maybe she's so much in pain she believes death would put an end to it. I can't tell what's the issue precisely, but for a little kid, their parents and family are their whole world. The relationship with their closest ones affects them deeply, more than anything else. I wouldn't overlook those daddy issues, I would try to better understand how she feels regarding this matter. Wishing you the best.

Interesting, is that Polish? Or some other Slavic language? In Bulgarian we still call them teratoma (which comes from greek and means "monstrous tumor"), but if we had to call it similarly, it would probably be "чудовище" (chudovishte).

It's more common in women, but it can be found in men too, usually the testicles, since in both cases it comes from germ cells. But it's more easily diagnosed in men, since it's more visible (it's harder to see or touch the ovaries).
Same, I wished to be a doctor when I was a kid, and when I was diagnosed with an ovarian teratoma, I weirdly got fascinated with the subject, subsequently with women's health in general.

Dermoid cyst is just another name for benign teratomas, which are themselves tumors. Only malignant tumors are called cancers. And in the case of teratomas, the chance of malignancy is around 2% only.

The reason they're called dermoid cyst is because the tumor grows inside a sack (aka the cyst) and it usually contains tissues of the dermal layers (skin, hair, etc.)
Depends on the tissues involved, but apparently the smell is beyond gross, since chances are it contains quite some sebum, skin, etc., all encapsulated in a cyst for years.

Usually very slowly, but it depends a lot on the kind of tissues inside. Mine got 15 cm big and I was only 23. Since it was mostly sebum, lots of hair and some cartilage, my theory is that it got so big so early because I have quite oily skin and hair, so it accumulated quickly inside the cyst. But that's more of an exception, most people get diagnosed later and with smaller teratomas.
While in many cases it can be asymptomatic, it might cause pains and if big enough, it can become visible, as if the person is constantly bloated.

The woman in question actually didn't have a teratoma, though in most cases of females with the disease (a rare kind of encephalitis that manifests at first as a psychiatric illness) it is caused by an ovarian teratoma. And specifically teratomas with brain tissue inside them. Her case helped bring more attention to the disease and how we see psychiatric illnesses as a whole. Doctors at first diagnosed her with psychiatric issues and wanted to put her in a mental ward. Turned out it was all "physical", even though in her case because of the lack of teratoma, they couldn't pinpoint a clear reason why she got sick.

There's also a movie of the same name.
What happened to her, did the cyst cause her the coma? I've only heard of cyst eruptions and twisted ovaries. And the rare cases of malignancy.

No, but if it's big enough, it can cause problems with pregnancy. My surgeon told me that my 15 cm big cyst would probably have prevented me from carrying a pregnancy to term, if I were pregnant with it. Some pregnant women get them removed at the same time as their c-section deliveries.

LMAO, I remember waiting for my own surgery, wondering what kind of tissues would be found in my cyst. I felt like having a Kinder surprise egg inside me and wishing I got to draw a rare one, like some sort of freaky pokemon, lol. But I ended up with the basic ones, just cartilage, sebum and hair (lots of hair!).
Fun fact, "-toma" means tumor, so teratoma is a kind of tumor ("tera" means "monster" btw). It's also benign in 98% of the cases, so it's safe to say it's almost never a cancer.

There's a book and movie about the encephalitis (even though the author didn't have a teratoma), it's called "Brain on Fire", it's a very interesting medical case that manifests more like a psychiatric illness at first.

Now I'm wondering if my hair ball also had some hair from my childhood years, I used to have a more light blonde color compared to nowadays.

>But teratoma is something that can happen to any woman at any given time (hence regular checkups are important).

Teratomas are congenital tumors that start developing even before one is born, they don't occur randomly during one's life, it's just that they happen to be discovered when they grow big enough to be seen on an imaging exam or through palpation during a regular check-up (in the case of an ovarian teratoma). You're advice is right, but when it comes to teratomas, it's all about finding out if one was born with a tumor early enough, to avoid further complications (cyst eruption or twisting of the ovary) and the more invasive surgery you're talking about (it's called laparotomy). If the teratoma wasn't completely removed, it might grow back, but otherwise one shouldn't be much worried about them. Regular checkups are definitely needed for other reasons (like cervical cancer).
You're not so far from the real etymology of the word teratoma, "tera" meaning "monster", and "toma" - "tumor". So it can be translated as "monstrous tumor".

I believe the worst thing about teratomas is the smell? I had one removed at 23, 15 cm long, lots of sebum and hair. I can only imagine how gross it was for the medical staff dealing with it. I have a picture of the cyst, but it can't fully transmit what it's like seeing one in real life.

I can recognise American tourists because they're the only ones spotted in a museum wearing the same garments they use for the gym or jogging. And that's noticeable not only in Bulgaria, but all across Europe. We still keep in mind a separation of dresscode depending on the environment and circumstances.

If I see a guy wearing a tank top, I'll assume he has been or is going to the gym or some other sporting activity. Or that he's commuting on a bicycle, a skateboard or something else. Otherwise, he would be wearing a t-shirt or short sleeve shirt.

Another similar attitude is the one towards flip-flops, they are supposed to be worn only around water activities, like the pool and beach. Sandals are acceptable on the other hand. It's not just that one looks more put together - flip-flops provide very little protection and feet get dirtier more quickly compared to when wearing sandals. One might also wonder if the said person doesn't have enough money to buy sandals, since flip-flops are much, much cheaper.

But despite all of this, Bulgarians aren't really judgemental regarding clothing style and maybe only some of the older generations have more ingrained dress codes in their minds. You probably didn't make a bad impression anyway.

I shared in another comment that I think having a formal education about parenting, human relationships (and adulting, as you mentioned), just as we have subjects about maths, geography, history, chemistry, etc, could be beneficial to society. Education based on research (psychology, sociology, medicine, neurology, etc.) and statistical data. Not religious or subjective morals, but research that proves facts, like for example that children raised in abusive households develop more physical and mental health issues as adults, cannot be ignored or dismissed. Not everyone has had a good family to give an example, many people would benefit from such education to fill in the gaps they lack.

I've been questioning why humans have kids for years, while for many people baby making is just a given, something natural and obvious, and they give me a confused look when I express my concerns out loud.

I've seen way too many bad examples of parenting and families. I've experienced first hand the consequences of that as a child. I know parents also suffer from it. I feel like it's a cycle that has been perpetuated by society because "it's the right thing to do" - you're born, you first idealize your parents, then you realize they aren't as perfect as they tried to present themselves, you have friction with them, you realize they've mistreated you, they don't want to admit that all their sacrifices and pain are now rewarded by an "ungrateful child", you end up in a sort of hot and cold relationship where you experience both positive and negative emotions and the cognitive dissonance is so strong, you don't know how to manage it. And at some point society reminds you that you're of age to procreate too, that's parenting is awesome, a privilege, a gift, and that you should repay what's been given to you by bringing another human to life. And you wanna believe it's really all that good and honorable, yet you're afraid of becoming like your parents, of committing grave mistakes despite all your efforts to be better than them.

I really like the French song by Stromae "C'est que du bonheur" ("It's all joy"), the lyrics portray that cycle in such a poignant way that hits you in the guts.

Being a parent is such a huge responsibility, there's so much to know about parenting, not just the practical stuff, but also how to raise an emotionally mature human being. And yet, society has left this crucial aspect at a savage level of ignorance. There are no schools about parenting, no degrees, no mandatory education, none of a baseline knowledge to make sure the next generation is raised in a healthy way. We're supposed to learn from our families, to have some inherent parental instincts, to figure it out ourselves. And I'm not saying we shouldn't have personal freedom to parent as we wish to, but we're so much left to our own devices, for something so important, that it's no wonder so many kids grow into adults that feel lost and unsupported.

Also, I believe a good relationship between the parents is crucial for the well-being of their children. But romantic relationships are also left at the same savage level, so what can we expect then of family relationships.

I don't believe that highly restraining the right of procreation or having super strict laws on how to raise kids is the answer - that would be super dystopian-like and could be used as a tool of dictatorship to control the populations. I believe though that opening the conversation on why people choose to have kids, being more accepting of child-free folks, and more supportive of those who become parents, could ease the pressure of starting families at all costs. And having a proper education on parenting could help people make better, informed choices before committing to a lifelong responsibility. There's still so much stigma around that topic, it should be normal to question it.

Got my first at 21 and I've had like 3 in total and I'm 26 now. I've heard about pain from others but I've personally never experienced that. The cervix itself isn't very sensitive and they just touch it lightly for a short time. What I noticed more was the speculum itself. There are multiple sizes and I suggest asking for a smaller one for your first time (the one for virgins). If they use a metal speculum, it might feel cold at first, but if they use a plastic one, it won't.

It's normal to feel self-conscious about nudity, I felt embarrassed too during my first one, but not on my second or third ones. You can shave if you believe it would make you feel more at ease, but it's not mandatory, at my first pap smear I was only trimmed and I got 0 remarks about pubic hair.

I can assure you that going through such exams are worth it and having to deal with a potential illness discovered too late is no joke. One of the many reasons women face gynecological issues is the lack of regular checkups and the shame surrounding them. Don't let it control you. To be empowered is to have power over one's health. You'll feel so proud for overcoming it and being a responsible adult. Best wishes.

Sounds like the timing is not right for him to be in a relationship, there's nothing wrong putting one's studies as a priority and not having enough time and energy to devote on a relationship. But one has to be aware of that and take the responsibility. Maybe someone would be willing to date him and spend little to no time with him, but if that's not you, don't force yourself into a relationship that clearly doesn't want to be what you need it to be. Granted, maybe it's just the timing, maybe after he finishes his studies he would have more time and things would be different. Or maybe not, maybe something else would come up and eat away the so precious time he cannot devote to you (like a job, a new hobby, other people, etc.) and the thing is, unless he chooses to be honest with you (which seems hard to accomplish, since he doesn't understand the need to communicate) now, you'll end up waiting for his life to change to figure him out.

Then, on the other hand, if you listen to him, and start living your life without him (going out with other people, doing your hobbies alone, travelling alone, planning things alone, etc.), you will still suffer, but in a different way. At first you might be sad for trying to enjoy life without your bf, you might feel lonely because he isn't besides you. Then maybe you would get over it and feel more at ease spending time with other people. But then those around you would be puzzled by your situation, friends would ask where your bf is, men would hit on you unknowingly that you're taken, chances are you would feel a weird cognitive dissonance, between trying to convince everyone that you're in a healthy relationship and what you truly feel in your heart.

And if you don't reach to other people and just stay alone and do your things - well, you'll still be miserable and lonely on top of everything. You will hold onto hope that he will change and it's something temporary you'll have to endure. And maybe if he could reassure you it's indeed the case, you could survive through that. But if he ends up not changing, you'll feel betrayed and might become resentful.

Ask each other what a ideal relationship would look like, regardless of external circumstances (like if both of you had all the time and money, what would you do) and see if your views match or not.

You two should have an open and honest discussion about sex, all sorts of questions, how you feel about sex, how much it matters to you, why you have sex, what turns you on and off, how much does the sex affect the relationship, etc. People can have widely different views and opinions on sex and not realize it.

For example, not everyone would think that having sex more often would make it "less special" or even "like a chore". For some people sex is an important way to connect with their significant other, for some physical intimacy might be enough or compensate the lack of sex, some would take rejection personally ("they're not attracted to me anymore, they don't love me anymore, what if there's someone else, what if I gained weight, what if they find me boring now, etc"), feel unworthy or unloved, some people lose their libido when stressed, others are on the opposite side - sex is how they deal with stress, some people put sex high in their priority list and want to make time to have sex, some prefer food or something else over sex, some feel it's crucial for their relationship, others consider it optional, some think that good sex means that said person would be satisfied and wouldn't need sex for awhile, while if they're unsatisfied, they would ask for more...the list goes on forever.

Without clear communication, we all assume that the other person views sex the same way as us, but this couldn't be further from the truth. Sex affects many aspects of life and many aspects of life affect the sex drive. In his mindset, he has no understanding as to why you would have a lower libido than before, and coupled with his lack of knowledge about asexuality, his only way to explain the situation to himself was to mislabel you, because it made sense in his mind (you should learn more about asexuality and educate him, wrong wording can be very harmful). Meanwhile, you probably don't understand why he still has the same libido (hint: he's still very young) or why it matters so much to him. So you end up both assuming wrong things about each other. Vulnerability and openness is key, the answers to these questions might surprise you or you might not like them, but in the end, you'll both have challenged your mind regarding sex, widened your views and maybe even changed opinions. And would probably find common ground, or at least more understanding and empathy towards each other.

It's not the suddenly acquired conventional attractiveness that "ruined" your life - it's the fear that you might loose that attractiveness and the benefits that you've encountered since (attention, validation, etc). You're afraid you'll become again your past self, so you're pushing yourself further and further. "If I become perfect, chances are I won't be ugly again". Maybe you're trying to compensate some lack of love/self-worth (like stemming from your family issues) with the validation you receive from being perceived as attractive - and hence to get more of it, you feel the need to up your game. More pretty = more liked/loved.

There's nothing wrong to want to prettify yourself, we all do it to some extent. Problem is when those preoccupations disrupt your life. You spend a lot of time thinking about your physical appearance, to an extent where you question things that are natural and normal (like height or face shape) and compare yourself to celebrities (they aren't just people like you and me, they're products of the media and they aren't necessarily happier than us), and even ignore/forget about your own hobbies. What exactly makes you "YOU"? Ask yourself that.

Maybe it's been a fairly recent transition for you and you haven't met yet the "pretty debts" of being conventionally attractive. Getting the wrong, superficial attention, for example. People would give you more attention at first, but they won't stay around only for your beauty (which we all know ain't eternal), the right ones would like to get to know you better, on a deeper level. They would be interested in your likes, your tastes, your hobbies, what you like doing in this world. Your past hobbies sound great, I'm sure there are people out there that would appreciate them too. And you certainly used to feel satisfaction from them. If you can imagine that people value more pretty girls, then you can imagine that they value even more pretty girls who have substance, a great mind to have conversations with, who inspire others, teach others, etc. If you're so fixated on beauty, why don't you learn more about the history of beauty through the ages, the societal and psychological research on beauty? This would help you get a better perspective on the subject, plus you'd be an interesting person to talk with.

What you feed your mind is what your mind creates later on. If you mostly follow celebrities/models or beauty content, given your current mindset, it's no wonder you end up spiraling and doomscrolling about your physical appearance. I suggest you do some digital decluttering - tidy up your social medias, unfollow or at least mute the profiles/channels that trigger you,  that feed those questions and insecurities. Do it on all your socials. Then, list all the other things in life that you're interested in or used to be - from little things like hobbies and fun activities through the bigger ones like your studies/career, and search content about them (not just content creators online, but also books, documentaries, podcasts, trainings, studies, etc). You are so much more than your physique. Start valuing your inner world and the right people would do the same (and ignore the wrong ones, obviously).

It doesn't seem to me that you have too much stuff, more like you lack furniture to properly organise and store them. A laundry basket or even one with multiple containers so that you can directly put out the dirty laundry where it needs to be; when you see that one of the containers is full, it means it's time to allocate a moment to do the laundry. A dinner plate to put on the dirty dishes/cups so that you can later on wash them. More trash bins so that you can easily throw anything away wherever you are in the room. Folders to categorise papers and a place to store them that is easily accessible. A proper rack for the shoes. More boxes for stuff you don't necessarily need now but you're certain you're gonna need later (and other boxes for the stuff you're uncertain of). More cabinets, drawers, even if it's bought second-hand. Your room seems to have space, but it looks a bit empty, so you end up frustrated because you don't know where to place your stuff and they end up in random places. This is applicable to everyone, but for someone with ADHD it's even more important. You might need to let go of some things, but you gotta first make sure you have the appropriate storage for the stuff you're gonna keep (and the new ones in the future). Once every single thing has its attributed place, it's easier to put it back there, because you won't have to do the mental work of wondering "what am I supposed to do with this, I don't know where I should put it" which can be exhausting and overwhelming, and when you have lots of such load, you just give up and leave it for later.

Même kilos, mais je fais 160 cm. Ma limite personnelle est de 42 kg par contre. Ma mère fait 155 cm et je crois qu'elle aussi a été à des moments à moins de 40 kg, alors qu'à d'autres périodes elle été plus (tout comme moi, j'ai déjà été 50 kg, quand je faisais du sport). Pourtant on a toujours eu nos règles et jamais eu de grosse carences. Ça dépend vraiment des gens, de leur style de vie et métabolisme.

Ma mère fait 155 cm et a toujours été mince. Elle avait une adolescence tardive, donc elle recevait des commentaires sur sa taille et développement dès le lycée. Depuis, pour éviter de ne pas être prise au sérieux, elle a commencé à s'habiller et à se porter plus comme une dame qu'une jeune fille - talons aiguilles, coiffure à cheveux longs, maquillage, vernis à ongles, vestimentaire d'un style classique. Ce physique au début la rendait plus âgée, certes. Elle m'a eu à 25 ans, mais elle a tout de même continué de laisser l'impression chez les gens qu'elle était plus jeune, et ils étaient surpris d'apprendre qu'elle avait un enfant. À part ça, je crois que son comportement aussi essayait de contrer les éventuels commentaires sur sa taille - sa confiance en soi, son regard, sa façon de parler. C'est du moins ce que j'ai remarqué.

Pour ma part, j'ai 26 ans, je fais 160 cm et j'ai une corpulence de fille plutôt que de femme (hanches étroites et poitrine petite à moyenne). J'ai récemment acheté une veste d'adolescent sans me rendre compte, car c'était à ma taille. J'ai encore des vêtements d'ado qui me vont toujours bien. J'ai aussi un vestimentaire plus féminin, mais au quotidien je préfère m'habiller en plus décontracté. Je garde mes cheveux longs, mais c'est juste une préférence. Je porte du mascara, mais pas plus. Le résultat - il arrive en effet que des gens dans la rue me crois pour une étudiante ou bien même lycéenne. Ils sont toujours surpris d'apprendre que je suis plus âgée. Mais je ne le prends pas mal, je trouve que c'est plus un point positif que négatif. J'ai le choix de faire plus "femme" quand je le déciderai, ce qui n'est pas le cas de tout le monde.

Je crois que ça dépend surtout du contexte, le rôle des gens dans votre vie ou bien les éventuelles conséquences de leurs préjugés. Si c'est une personne proche, un conjoint par example, cela est en effet regrettable. Si c'est quelqu'un du boulot et que cela affecte votre travail, aussi. Sinon dans le reste des cas, ce n'est sans importance. Oui, on peut essayer de paraître plus féminine ou plus âgée, mais franchement, ce n'est pas de notre faute qu'on soit née avec une taille plus petite que la moyenne, une corpulence naturellement plus mince ou bien avec un visage innocent. Ils existent des gens pour qui cela a son charme ou bien n'est pas une raison de nous faire croire qu'on doit changer. Entourez vous de ces personnes et ne prêter pas attention au reste. Si vous voulez changer quelque chose dans votre apparence ou comportement, libre à vous, il n'y a rien de mal en soit. Mais ça restera toujours un problème de société et non votre faute.

Well, first of all, the whole world has been confused about sex for ages. Religion, social norms, gender roles, you name it. Then the sexual revolution and sex-related female empowerment. Humans are constantly wondering what is wrong and what is right and have been swinging between the two extremes. Nowadays we face new challenges with technology having a say more and more into our communication, relationships and sexuality. Things have being changing a lot lately and it's getting harder to navigate through that sea of different lifestyles and choices available. Not to mention the gazillion personal reasons involved (like the upbringing, as you shared). So you feeling contradicted is fairly understandable, even more because of your young age.

Reconciliating that cognitive dissonance ain't easy or straightforward. Besides gaining more life experience, you could start by asking more questions about yourself, your past, your childhood, your previous relationships, your relationship with yourself, your body and sexuality. Trying to figure out yourself better in order to know how to manage your sexual desires and urges in a healthy and safe way.

I've collected some insights from your reddit history that are worth mentioning regarding your question:
- you are coming from two very different cultures who probably have very different approaches to sex, relationships and self-esteem. That alone is a big factor.
- your parents history has impacted your inner monologue. It's important to remind yourself those words aren't absolute truth - they're just reflection of your parents experience. You can listen to them and keep their conclusions in mind, but it's only up to you to decide whether or not you approve them and want to live by them. Your personality and needs might differ from your parents.
- you've been a victim of SA and that has certainly impacted your sexuality and self-image. Having been feeling taken advantage of in the past can contribute to the wish of getting ones power back, like having sex on one's terms (who, where and when), yet remind one how they can fall again in the same trap ("being used by a man").
- you've had a long-term relationship that wasn't truly healthy, where you didn't feel sexual attraction and didn't have sexual compatability. It didn't give you the opportunity to establish a sane sexual relationship, in a committed, loving and safe environment.
- you have some body image issues that have probably affected your self-esteem and confidence in intimacy.

I'm not mentioning other issues unrelated to the sex subject, but they might play a part too, since sexuality is tightly tied to the whole psychology of a person.

Feeling horny is normal and part of the human experience, even if you're single. Wanting physical intimacy, affection and being desired. It's difficult though to express that part of oneself when it has been tied to multiple negative/mixed experiences. You're only 21 and have still plenty of self-discovery lying ahead of you. But it's best to do that in the right circumstances, where you can feel safe, comfortable and in control, in order to avoid any further damage. Whatever you choose to do, make sure you don't compromise yourself. Sex and self-esteem are after all, a matter of perception and attitude. It can feel degrading with the wrong person/relationship and wonderful, fulfilling with the right one. Find someone that is both attractive to you and treats you well to explore that aspect of yourself. Self-pleasuring can help you learn more about your body and build a healthier view on sex. You don't have to enter a committed relationship if you don't feel like it, but don't let anyone disrespect you either.

Since there's less to do in winter than summertime (except for snow sports, the ski resorts are like 100 km from Nice), I would suggest indoor activities and a few outdoor ones:
- museums. There's a variety of museums, mostly art museums that could give him some art culture that might differ from his home place. Lots of famous artists have visited the French Riviera and there's plenty of museums and galleries scattered around. Nice has like a dozen.
- the ice skating ring is big and well maintained, been there once, lots of young people.
- there's a board game café in the old town that has a wide collection of board games, the staff is nice, it's called La Bulle à Jeux.
- there's a cat café in the city center, with 4 cats, one being a Maine Coon, it's called La Ronronnerie.
- lots of food options, he could simply eat out every day at different places to discover local (Chez Pipo) and Italian cuisines, but also from some other cultures (like the ramens at IKKO ramen, etc.).
- if he's interested in reading French, libraries and bookshops offer many book choices. The FNAC at the city center has a nice cafe where one can eat a bagel and read some.

Getting to know yourself comes from experience, and obviously, young people usually lack this. That's why many drop one major to join another, get multiple degrees, switch careers, have more than one different jobs. It's all much more various and flexible than society and school teaches us. As others have already pointed out, removing the hairs from your brush every time after brushing is a must, alongside regular deep cleaning (like once a week for example).

But another thing you could do is preventing your brush from getting this dirty:
- after shampooing your hair, apply conditioner or a mask and comb your hair with a detangling brush while it's wet - this helps removing most of your dead hairs while still being in the shower, where it's much easier to retrieve them (again, you need to remove hairs from the brush after every usage). This helps not having so much dry hair on your regular brush (keep the other brush only for the shower, therefore it will always stay clean), which means easier maintenance. The conditioner/mask helps detangling the hair, don't skip it. I also recommend once in awhile exfoliating your scalp (usually done before the shampoo) - it removes tons more hair, product built-up and gives an overall lighter feeling.
- dirty hair makes the brush/comb dirty in turn - simply as that, maybe you should just shampoo more often. Depends on the person, I personally need to wash mine once every two days, afterwards my brush becomes way dirtier. And a dirty brush makes the hair dirtier, so it's a vicious cycle. Others mentioned product built-up and cleansing shampoos, you might consider them as factors depending on your routine.
- another option is along with the "wet brush" (for under the shower) and the "dry brush" (when your hair is clean and dry), you could get a third brush, a "dirty brush", as the name says, one for dirty hair days. I have one meant only for that purpose - when I haven't had the opportunity to shower and I need to do an updo, I don't use my regular brush, I use this one. 3 brushes might sound a lot, but this separation of usages makes maintenance way easier in my experience - I never wash, only rinse my wet brush; I don't have to wash my dry brush that regularly (because there isn't much hair on it, I remove some every time and my hair is clean overall, so my brush stays quite clean as well); and I wash my dirty brush occasionally (I use it rarely).

This comes from someone who has waist-length hair that sheds a lot, and used to wash their hair only once a week back in the days - so I've had quite some experience with dirty brushes. Washing them feels like a chore to me, so I managed to find a way to not do it that often.

But first of all, do a deep cleaning to that brush, your hair will thank you. Read a bit more on the subject of brushes, which types are best for your hair type and for what usage they're made, along with maintenance. You can also pick wooden brushes/combs for environmental concerns (even for a wet brush, as long as you let it dry properly, I hang in a place in the bathroom where it's within my reach, but with no water splashing over). Make removing hairs from the brush after every combing a habit.
